content.p: In the early hours of Sunday 12 June 2016, a gunman walked into Pulse, a gay nightclub on South Orange Avenue in Orlando, Florida, and opened fire on a crowd that was winding down a Latin-themed night. By the time police killed him, roughly three hours later, 49 people were dead, making it the deadliest mass shooting in modern American history up to that point, as CNN and History.com described it. CNN put the number of wounded at 53.

The man responsible, 29-year-old Omar Mateen, was a licensed security guard who had been questioned by the FBI in earlier years. During the siege he telephoned 911 to pledge allegiance to the Islamic State. Why he picked this club has never been settled. His widow, Noor Salman, was tried in federal court in 2018 and acquitted on every count.
content.h2: A Latin night on Orange Avenue
content.p: Reports differ on the size of the crowd: CNN gave some 320 people, History.com nearly 300. The music was Latin, the room was busy, and the evening was ending. History.com quoted survivors who said they did not at first realise what the noise was. Jon Alamo told the BBC that he heard "20, 40, 50 shots" and that "the music stopped".

CNN's timeline places the first gunfire at about 1:58 a.m., in the middle of the club. Clubgoer Patience Carter said she and her friends had just agreed to order a ride home when they heard it, and they ran for a bathroom. At around 2:02 a.m. an officer who was working an off-duty shift in uniform at the club engaged the gunman. According to CNN, he felt outgunned, backed out of the building and called for help. A police presentation obtained by a local television station and reported by CBS News named him as Officer Adam Gruler; it said he called an officer-needs-help signal and fired at Mateen in the doorway.

Two SWAT officers in a nearby patrol car joined the gunfight, CNN reported, and other patrol officers went in while it was going on to pull survivors out. Mateen backed away down a hallway, exchanged fire with a SWAT lieutenant and barricaded himself in a bathroom with a group of clubgoers. Over the following 45 minutes, about 100 deputies and city officers converged on the scene.

The first hour is told largely through the phones of people who were inside. At 2:06 a.m., CBS News reported, a young man named Eddie Justice texted his mother: "Mommy I love you." Two minutes later he wrote "I'm gonna die." She asked which bathroom he was in; he replied that "He has us" and that police needed to come and get them. At 2:49 he wrote "Hurry," then "He's in the bathroom with us." His last message to her was a single word, "Yes".

At 2:09 the club itself posted on Facebook: "Everyone get out of Pulse and keep running." Another victim's call to 911 at about 2:20 confirmed that Mateen was in one of two adjoining bathrooms with hostages, according to the Crime Museum. CNN wrote that police knew there were hostages once clubgoers trapped in the bathroom got word out to them.
content.h2: What the gunman said on the phone
content.p: CNN placed Mateen's first calls to 911 at roughly 2:22 a.m., when it said he called three times, hanging up on one and speaking briefly on another. The Crime Museum and the International Code of Conduct Association put his call to a 911 operator later, at 2:35 a.m. CBS News, which said the call lasted about 50 seconds, published the FBI's transcript, in which he said he was in Orlando, that he had done "the shootings", and pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi of the Islamic State. CNN added that he mentioned the Boston Marathon bombers and a Florida man who had died as a suicide bomber in Syria. Patience Carter told CNN that he also said he wanted America to stop bombing his country.

The gunman then spoke three times with the Orlando police Crisis Negotiation Team, calls lasting about nine, 16 and three minutes, according to CBS. When a negotiator asked what he had done, CBS reported, he answered: "No, you already know what I did." He claimed that a vehicle outside held bombs. He said he had a vest of the kind "used in France". CNN reported that he also threatened to strap explosive vests to four hostages and detonate them within 15 minutes, and that around 2:45 a.m. he phoned a local television station, News 13 Orlando, and said he had acted for the Islamic State.
content.h2: Three hours of waiting, then the wall
content.p: The wait drew questions. CNN reported that police later said they had needed the time to assess the situation, bring up armoured vehicles and make sure they had enough personnel. During this period, CNN said, police did not exchange fire with Mateen, and officers kept bringing people out. Eight people escaped when officers removed an air-conditioning unit and they crawled through the gap. Others were led out when officers smashed down a door, freeing about 30 people.

At around 5:00 a.m. the approach changed. SWAT officers set off an explosive charge to open a wall, but according to CNN it was only partly effective, and an armoured vehicle was used to widen the hole. The opening led to a hallway rather than the bathroom. The Crime Museum added that the noise alarmed Mateen, who shot three more hostages. Police responded with stun and flash grenades to draw him out. CNN said he then left the bathroom and began firing at officers, who returned fire and killed him. The Crime Museum recorded the time as 5:17 a.m. Police told the public at 5:53 a.m. on social media that the shooter was dead. Orlando's police chief, John Mina, later said one officer was struck on his helmet and saved by it.

The police presentation reported by CBS in April 2017 contained a count of where victims died: nine in the north bathroom, where Mateen was barricaded for much of the standoff, four in the south bathroom, and eleven in hospital or triage areas set up outside. Nearly half of the 49 died on the dance floor, it said. The Crime Museum gave a different split, 38 at the scene and 11 after reaching hospital. Mina said he did not know whether any victim had been hit by police gunfire.

Mateen was identified at about 10:15 a.m. as a 29-year-old from Fort Pierce, Florida, in CNN's timeline; CBS gave his town as Port St. Lucie. He worked as a guard for G4S. The International Code of Conduct Association wrote that he had been interviewed by the FBI in 2013 and 2014 after reports of extremist behaviour, including false claims of links to the Boston Marathon bombers, al-Qaeda and Hezbollah; the allegations were judged insubstantial. History.com said he was questioned twice in 2013 and again in 2014 over a possible link to Moner Mohammad Abu-Salha, an American who carried out a suicide bombing in Syria. The Crime Museum said he had been placed on a terrorist watchlist and investigated for almost a year.

The association's case study also reported, as allegations, that a former co-worker had complained repeatedly to G4S about Mateen's remarks and quit because of harassment, and that G4S kept Mateen on without a fresh psychological evaluation after the FBI interviews. Florida later fined G4S $151,400 for providing inaccurate information on forms that allow employees to carry guns, the largest penalty on record under that state law. A civil suit by victims, survivors and their representatives claimed that the firm should be liable, but a judge dismissed it in April 2019 on the ground that Mateen was not working for G4S at the time.

Motive remains disputed. The Crime Museum noted that Mateen left no manifesto and was killed at the scene, and that investigators did not believe the Islamic State had coordinated the attack. History.com wrote that his family said he had shown anger at two gay men kissing a week earlier, but that evidence emerging after the attack suggested a planned act of terrorism and possibly a different target. During the 2018 trial, federal prosecutors said in closing that Mateen had meant to target Disney Springs on the night of 11 June but was put off by law enforcement officers there. ClickOrlando reported that phone and search records showed he then searched for "downtown Orlando nightclubs" and probably did not know that Pulse served a gay clientele. The Crime Museum also reported claims by witnesses that he had been a regular at Pulse, which, it said, investigators found nothing to confirm.

Noor Salman, who was 31 at trial, was arrested in January 2017 and charged with aiding and abetting material support of a foreign terrorist organisation and with obstructing justice. Prosecutors said she helped Mateen beforehand and lied to the FBI to impede the inquiry. Assistant US Attorney Sara Sweeney told the jury that Salman "didn't pull the trigger that night, but she did serve as a green light for her husband."

Jurors heard about 10 days of testimony and saw surveillance video of Mateen buying weapons and of a shopping trip with Salman at least a week before the attack. A statement she wrote after her arrest, shown in court, said: "I wish I had done the right thing, but my fear held me back." FBI special agent Ricardo Enriquez testified that she told investigators Mateen had watched jihadi beheading videos, bought a rifle and ammunition and visited a gun range. The defence called her a mother and a victim of Mateen's abuse and infidelity, and of coercive questioning. A forensic psychologist, Bruce Frumkin, testified that she had been interviewed for 11 hours and that her IQ score was 84. Her lawyer Linda Moreno told jurors: "Omar Mateen is a monster. Noor Salman is a mother, not a monster."

Late in the trial the defence learned that Mateen's father, Seddique Mateen, had been a confidential FBI source at points between January 2005 and June 2016, and was under investigation over money transfers to Turkey and Afghanistan, according to a defence motion quoting an email from prosecutors. The judge denied a motion to dismiss, saying the information was not relevant. He was on the prosecution's witness list but was not called.

Jurors began deliberating on a Wednesday and returned on Friday 30 March 2018, finding Salman not guilty of both charges. She had faced life in prison. Orange County Sheriff Jerry Demings said many felt that justice had not prevailed; Pulse owner Barbara Poma said the verdict "cannot and will not divide us".
content.h2: After the shooting: scrutiny, lawsuits and a memorial
content.p: The April 2017 police presentation included self-assessments. Chief Mina said that fire department officials had not been in the police command post and that better communication might have helped, although "the people who needed care, got care". The presentation said fire department officials reported that many firefighters did not know police would use explosives to breach the building.

A week before the second anniversary, more than 35 victims and their lawyers filed a federal civil rights suit against the city of Orlando, its police department and Officer Gruler, alleging that their constitutional rights had been violated. ClickOrlando reported that the FBI described the shooting as an open and active investigation, even after the trial ended.

A temporary memorial opened about a month before the second anniversary, the first official place for mourners at the site since the FBI put a fence around it, and a bell was due to toll 49 times at First United Methodist Church on the anniversary, ClickOrlando said. A rainbow crosswalk in front of the club was painted over the year before the demolition, after a Florida Department of Transportation memo barred "surface art", as the Inquirer recounted. The city of Orlando bought the Pulse property in 2023 for $2 million, following a failed years-long effort by a foundation run by the club's former owner to acquire it. Demolition began on 18 March 2026, with a $12 million permanent memorial planned to open in 2027.
